aAbout: Google Earth is the world's most detailed free virtual globe: high-resolution satellite and aerial imagery, 3D cities and terrain, Street View at ground level, a historical-imagery archive reaching back decades, and tools for measuring, drawing and telling stories with places (including guided Voyager tours and Google Earth Studio for animations). Google Earth Pro — once $399/year — has been free since 2015. Everything in it is archival: the imagery shows the world as it was photographed, not as it is now.
aStrengths: Google Earth is the gold standard for exploring a place: the most detailed 3D cities anywhere, Street View, the deepest historical imagery archive (decades back), powerful measurement and drawing tools, KML/KMZ data import and Earth Studio for cinematic animations — all permanently free. Nobody matches its imagery depth, 3D building coverage and the familiarity billions of users already have.
bAbout: NASA Worldview is NASA EOSDIS's free, open-source browser for near-real-time satellite imagery: more than 1,000 global, full-resolution layers — fires, storms, air quality, sea ice, vegetation and more — most updated within about three hours of observation, some spanning nearly 30 years. It adds event pins for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions, time-lapse animation building, layer comparison (swipe and opacity) and downloadable underlying data via NASA's GIBS services. No signup; it runs in the browser.
bStrengths: NASA Worldview is an extraordinary free research tool: 1,000+ full-resolution satellite layers, most refreshed within ~3 hours, geostationary imagery in 10-minute increments, event tracking for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions, custom time-lapse animations and comparison tools — open source, backed by NASA's EOSDIS, with the data itself downloadable. For environmental science and disaster analysis, its scientific layer library is unmatched at any price, let alone free.
betterAnswer: They answer different questions. Google Earth is better for places: what does this address, coastline or city look like, in 3D, at street level, and how did it change over the decades? NASA Worldview is better for processes: what is happening across the planet's systems right now — the fire, the storm, the ice edge, the algal bloom. If you only keep one bookmark, keep the one matching your question — researchers keep both, and both are free.

intro: Google Earth and NASA Worldview both show you the planet from space, completely free — and they could hardly be more different. Google Earth is the beautiful archive: the deepest collection of satellite and aerial imagery ever assembled, wrapped in a 3D globe with cities and Street View. NASA Worldview is the live instrument: over a thousand scientific satellite layers refreshed within hours, built for watching fires, storms, ice and oceans change. One shows the world as it was; the other, as it nearly is.
pricingA: Completely free — Google Earth Pro (once $399/year) has been free since 2015. No paid tiers, no subscriptions; a Google account is optional.
pricingB: Completely free — NASA provides Worldview as a public service through EOSDIS. No paid plans, and no signup is required to browse.

verdictA: Choose Google Earth if you explore places — checking a neighbourhood, a coastline or a construction site, walking streets in 3D, measuring land, or watching a familiar place change across decades of imagery.
verdictB: Choose NASA Worldview if you watch systems — tracking a wildfire's spread, a hurricane's approach, sea-ice retreat or air-quality plumes with imagery that is hours old, not years.
worldEye: WorldEye takes a third position: a free 3D globe whose satellite view is combined with live data — flights, ships, 74,229 public cameras, weather, earthquakes and wildfires — so you see imagery and activity together, with no signup. Its imagery is neither Google Earth's archive nor NASA's science library, and it doesn't claim to be; it's the live-planet view. An optional Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds the OSINT toolkit and intel feeds.
